newsitem.title: UK: Scotland kicks off world's biggest arts festival.
newsitem.headline: Scotland kicks off world's biggest arts festival.

text.p: Edinburgh kicked off the world's biggest celebration of the arts on Sunday with 50th birthday International, Fringe and Film festivals cramming every theatre, church hall and street corner of the Scottish capital.
Thousands of actors, musicians, comedians and dancers started a hectic three-week jamboree of round the clock entertainment that promises to delight many and disgust a few.

Born amid the ruins and disillusion of World War Two, the Edinburgh International Festival, and the Fringe and Film festivals that grew up alongside, have turned into a world showcase of the arts that now far outstrips in scale the music festivals of Bayreuth and Salzburg it once dared to emulate.
Until August 30, arts lovers can breakfast on Shakespeare, heckle stand-up comedians on the back of a lorry, pore over the best in pop videos, and enjoy a Spanish multi-media soap opera.

A star-studded cast of celebrity performers and guests includes native Scot Sean Connery, actor Michael Caine, film director Mike Leigh, actor-director Steven Berkoff, and American dancer-choreographer Mark Morris.
The 5.8 million pound ($9.2 million) International festival boasts its first appearance since 1961 by the Royal Opera Covent Garden, and four world premieres in dance, music and theatre.

The Royal Opera, without a home following the closure of its London Covent Garden theatre for a 2-1/2 year, 214 million pound redevelopment scheme, presents a new production of Jean-Philippe Rameau's 18th century opera "Platee".
With costumes by U.S. fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi, it is expected to be one of the highlights of the festival.
A strong dance programme sees the first British visit in 17 years of the San Francisco ballet, two new works by Twyla Tharp and the British debut of Australia's Bangarra Dance Theatre.
The Fringe, which started in 1947 with eight companies upset at being left out of the main festival, has mushroomed to 1,278 shows from as far afield as New Zealand and New York.

No subject matter is taboo for the often anarchic, no-vetting Fringe. Its 1997 offerings range from a show about air traffic controllers to a midnight performance of Angela Carter's erotic "Bluebeard" tale in Edinburgh's underground vaults.

"Even reading the Fringe programme is an exhilarating experience. The talent, passion, energy and imagination involved in making this fabulous event happen is jumping off the pages. The Fringe is on its finest form yet," said Fringe director Hilary Strong.

The film festival -- once described by late American director John Huston as the "only film festival that's worth a damn" -- features 300 movies, including U.S. director Spike Lee's civil rights documentary "Four Little Girls".
The pop video is raised to a new art form through a special section dedicated to music promotion films, and British actor Alan Rickman delivers a celebrity lecture.

The 50th birthday is also marked by reproduction of a series of archive recordings of music performances during the early years of the festival, including opera by the late Maria Callas, and concerts conducted by the late Benjamin Britten and Leonard Bernstein. ($ = 0.629 British Pounds)
